はじめまして — Nice to meet you
You introduce yourself, say where you’re from and what you do, and ask simple questions.
nice to meet you / I’m counting on you
To introduce yourself politely: はじめまして、〜です。よろしく おねがいします。
To use the basic sentence: X は Y です (X is Y).
To make negative sentences: じゃ ありません.
To ask questions with か and answer with はい / いいえ.
To use the particle の: わたし の せんせい (my teacher).
To say nationality (〜じん) and language (〜ご).

Japanese distinguishes between short and long vowels. ō (written おう or とう) is held twice as long: Tōkyō = “Toh-kyoh”, arigatō = “arigatoh”. If you shorten it, it can become a different word!
After s and k, the u is barely heard: です = “des”, ます = “mas”, すごい = “s-goi”. Japanese people speak like that naturally.
ん is a whole syllable, with its own length: せんせい = “se-n-se-i” (4 beats). Don’t swallow it.
Every syllable has the same length, like a metronome: ha-ji-me-ma-shi-te. Japanese has no strong stress like English, just a pitch that rises or falls slightly.
1. The basic sentence: X は Y です
This is the most important sentence in Japanese. X は Y です means “X is Y”.
Step by step: は (read “wa”, even though it’s written like “ha”!) shows WHAT we’re talking about. です comes at the end and means “is / am / are”, politely.
Great news: Japanese has NO articles (a, the), NO genders (masculine / feminine) and the verb does NOT change with the person. です is the same for “I am”, “you are”, “she is”!
Unlike English, “I” is usually left out: “ミハイ です” = “(I’m) Mihai”. Japanese people rarely say わたし.
The verb ALWAYS goes at the end of the sentence. Japanese word order is “I Mihai am”.
2. The negative: じゃ ありません
For “is not”, replace です with じゃ ありません (ja arimasen).
In written or very formal texts you’ll see では ありません (de wa arimasen). It means exactly the same.
To make a question, add か (ka) at the end. That’s all! The word order doesn’t change. In traditional writing you don’t even use a “?”.
はい、そう です。 (hai, sō desu)
いいえ、ちがいます。 (iie, chigaimasu)
そう です か。 (sō desu ka)
“そう です か” with a falling tone = “ah, I see”. Japanese people use it constantly in conversation to show they’re listening.
の (no) links two nouns. The first describes the second. The order is like English “’s”: the describing word comes first!
Tip: read “A の B” like English “A’s B”: “A’s B” / “B of A”.
You can link several: ミハイさん の にほんご の せんせい = Mihai’s Japanese teacher.
The rule is very simple: country + じん (jin) = the person; country + ご (go) = the language.
〜さん (-san) goes after another person’s name, out of politeness, for men and women alike: ミハイさん, ゆきさん. It’s like “Mr / Ms”, but used far more often.
NEVER put さん after your own name! Saying “ミハイさん です” about yourself sounds silly.
6. Why do some words look different? Katakana
Have you noticed that ミハイ, ルーマニア, スペイン look different? They’re written in KATAKANA, the second Japanese script, used for foreign names and words.
Every hiragana sign has a katakana “sibling” with the same sound: あ = ア, い = イ, か = カ… You’ll find them all in the kana table (the あ Kana button).
The long line ー lengthens the vowel: ルーマニア = Ruu-mania.
You don’t need to know katakana yet. Every word has its romaji transcription underneath. We’ll learn it systematically in the next chapters.
は (wa) marks who we’re talking about.
か at the end = a question.
わたし の せんせい = my teacher.
